steps.title: Telling a driver where to go
steps.how_to: How to tell someone you call Lei what to do, like a taxi driver.
steps.intro: This is how you ask someone you call Lei to do something, like a taxi driver or a stranger in the street. It uses the same forms as the present subjunctive.

examples.said: Giri alla prima a destra, per favore.
Vada un po' più avanti, per favore.
Vada sempre dritto, poi giri a destra.
examples.en: Go straight ahead, then turn right.

examples.said: Prenda il primo autobus.

steps.notice: With Lei, verbs ending in -are take an -i (giri) and the others take an -a (prenda), the opposite of the tu forms; andare becomes vada. That's because this command is really the subjunctive.
steps.context: In most Italian cities you take a taxi from a rank or book one by phone or app.

ask.said: Un turista anziano ti chiede la strada per la piazza. Cosa gli dici?
ask.en: An older tourist asks you the way to the piazza. What do you tell him?

answer.said: Vada sempre dritto, poi giri a destra.
answer.en: Go straight ahead, then turn right.

ask.said: Sei in taxi e il tassista non conosce la tua via. Cosa gli dici?
ask.en: You're in a taxi and the driver doesn't know your street. What do you tell him?

answer.said: Giri alla prima a destra e vada più avanti.
answer.en: Take the first right and keep going.

ask.said: Una signora vuole andare in centro in autobus. Cosa le dici?
ask.en: A woman wants to take the bus downtown. What do you tell her?

mission.goal: Give a taxi driver directions to your street.

say.said: Giri alla prima a destra, per favore.

steps.title: Have a seat, how can I help
steps.how_to: How to place mi and si when you ask someone you call Lei to do something.
steps.intro: Today you'll learn the polite phrases staff use with you, like mi dica and si accomodi, and how to say them yourself. With Lei, the little words mi and si come first.

examples.said: Buongiorno, mi dica.
examples.en: Good morning, how can I help you?

examples.said: Prego, si accomodi.
Mi porti in via Veneto, per favore.
examples.en: Take me to Via Veneto, please.

examples.said: Mi faccia anche la ricevuta, per favore.
examples.en: Could I get a receipt too, please?

steps.notice: With Lei, mi and si always go before the verb: mi dica, si accomodi, mi porti. That's different from tu commands like dimmi, where they go on the end.
steps.context: At the end of a taxi ride, you can ask the driver for a receipt, la ricevuta.

ask.said: Una signora anziana entra e cerca una sedia. Cosa le dici?
ask.en: An older woman comes in, looking for a chair. What do you say to her?

ask.said: Sei in taxi e vuoi andare in via Veneto. Cosa dici al tassista?
ask.en: You're in a taxi and you want to go to Via Veneto. What do you tell the driver?

answer.said: Mi porti in via Veneto, per favore.
answer.en: Take me to Via Veneto, please.

ask.said: Lavori in un ufficio e arriva un signore. Cosa gli dici?
ask.en: You work in an office and a man comes in. What do you say to him?

answer.en: Good morning, how can I help you?

mission.goal: Offer an older neighbor a seat.

steps.title: Telling someone not to worry
steps.how_to: How to tell someone you call Lei not to do something.
steps.intro: Now you'll tell someone you call Lei not to do something, most often not to worry. You'll hear non si preoccupi all the time.

examples.said: Non si preoccupi, Le tengo io il posto.
examples.en: Don't worry, I'll save your seat.

examples.said: Non si preoccupi, glielo prendo io.
examples.en: Don't worry, I'll take it in for you.

examples.said: Non lo tocchi, per favore.
Non se ne vada, arrivo subito!
examples.en: Don't leave, I'll be right with you!

steps.notice: Put non in front of the same polite form and keep si or lo before the verb: non si preoccupi, non lo tocchi. Nothing else changes.

ask.said: Il tuo vicino aspetta un pacco, ma domani non è a casa. Cosa gli dici?
ask.en: Your neighbor is expecting a package, but he won't be home tomorrow. What do you tell him?

answer.said: Non si preoccupi, glielo prendo io.
answer.en: Don't worry, I'll take it in for you.

ask.said: In sala d'attesa, una signora deve uscire un momento. Cosa le dici?
ask.en: In the waiting room, a woman needs to step out for a moment. What do you tell her?

answer.said: Non si preoccupi, Le tengo io il posto.
answer.en: Don't worry, I'll save your seat.

ask.said: Lavori in un negozio e un cliente vuole andare via. Cosa gli dici?
ask.en: You work in a shop and a customer wants to leave. What do you tell him?

answer.said: Non se ne vada, arrivo subito!
answer.en: Don't leave, I'll be right with you!

mission.goal: Reassure an older neighbor who needs a hand.

say.said: Non si preoccupi, glielo prendo io.
say.en: Don't worry, I'll take it in for you.

steps.title: Come in, take your time
steps.how_to: How to make a polite command sound like a friendly invitation.
steps.intro: Today you'll turn a polite command into a warm invitation, the way people do when they ask you in or tell you to take your time. Two small words do it: pure and prego.

examples.said: Entri pure!
Faccia pure con calma.
Prego, si sieda.
Mi dia pure la borsa, gliela tengo io.
examples.en: Go ahead and give me your bag, I'll hold it for you.

steps.notice: Pure after the verb, or prego before it, makes a command sound like an invitation. Here pure means "go ahead," not "also."

ask.said: Un vicino anziano bussa alla tua porta e dice: "Permesso?" Cosa rispondi?
ask.en: An older neighbor knocks on your door and says, "May I come in?" What do you say?

ask.said: Una signora cerca i soldi e ti chiede scusa. Cosa le dici?
ask.en: A woman is looking for her money and apologizes to you. What do you tell her?

ask.said: Una signora anziana ha una borsa pesante. Cosa le offri?
ask.en: An older woman has a heavy bag. What do you offer her?

answer.said: Mi dia pure la borsa, gliela tengo io.
answer.en: Go ahead and give me your bag, I'll hold it for you.

mission.goal: Invite an older neighbor into your home.

steps.title: A few, everyone, something
steps.how_to: How to say a few, everyone and something with qualche, ognuno and qualcosa di.
steps.intro: These words help you talk about how many or which ones without counting: a few minutes, everyone, something hot. You'll hear them at counters and in waiting rooms.

examples.said: Aspetti qualche minuto, arrivo subito.
examples.en: Wait a few minutes, I'll be right with you.

examples.said: C'è qualche problema?
Ognuno ha il suo numero: adesso tocca al quarantadue.
examples.en: Everyone has a number, and now it's forty-two's turn.

examples.said: Desidera qualcosa di caldo?

steps.notice: Qualche means "a few" or "some" but always takes a singular noun: qualche minuto. Ognuno means "everyone," and qualcosa di plus a describing word means "something" of that kind.

ask.said: Dal medico, di solito quanto aspetti?
ask.en: How long do you usually wait at the doctor's?

answer.en: I usually wait a few minutes.

ask.said: Fa freddo e sei al bar. Cosa vuoi bere?
ask.en: It's cold and you're at the bar. What do you want to drink?

ask.said: In sala d'attesa, come sai quando tocca a te?
ask.en: In the waiting room, how do you know when it's your turn?

say.said: Vorrei qualcosa di caldo, per favore.

b1-10.title: Work, study and a language course

steps.title: Asking the right question
steps.how_to: How to ask which, how much, how come and how long.
steps.intro: Today you'll ask the questions that come up when you sign up for a course or meet someone new. Each question word asks for something different.

examples.said: Quali sono i Suoi punti di forza?
Da quanto tempo studia l'italiano?
examples.en: How long have you been studying Italian?

examples.said: Come mai proprio in Italia?
Quanto dura il corso e quanto costa?
examples.en: How long is the course, and how much does it cost?

steps.notice: Quali sono asks "what are" when you choose from a set, like strengths. Come mai means "how come," and da quanto tempo asks how long something has been going on.

ask.said: Vuoi sapere il prezzo di un corso. Cosa chiedi?
ask.en: You want to know the price of a course. What do you ask?

answer.en: How much does the course cost?

ask.said: Una signora parla molto bene l'inglese. Cosa le chiedi?
ask.en: A woman speaks English very well. What do you ask her?

answer.en: How long have you been studying English?

ask.said: Un signore americano vive qui da poco. Cosa gli chiedi?
ask.en: An American man has just moved here. What do you ask him?

mission.goal: At a language school, ask how long the course lasts and what it costs.

say.said: Quanto dura il corso e quanto costa?
say.en: How long is the course, and how much does it cost?

steps.title: How long, then and now
steps.how_to: How to say how long you did something, and how long you've been doing it.
steps.intro: Now you'll say how long you did something in the past and how long you've been doing something now. Italian uses per for the first and da for the second.

examples.said: Ho lavorato per vent'anni come ingegnere.
examples.en: I worked as an engineer for twenty years.

examples.said: Ho lavorato per dieci anni nel turismo.
examples.en: I worked in tourism for ten years.

examples.said: Studio l'italiano da un anno.
examples.en: I've been studying Italian for a year.

examples.said: Vivo in Italia da due anni.
examples.en: I've been living in Italy for two years.

steps.notice: For something that's over, use the past with per: ho lavorato per vent'anni. For something still going on, use the present with da, because it hasn't stopped: studio da un anno.

ask.said: Che lavoro facevi prima?
ask.en: What did you do for work before?

answer.en: I worked as a … for … years.

ask.said: È tanto che studi l'italiano?
ask.en: Have you been studying Italian long?

ask.said: Da quanto tempo vivi in questa città?
ask.en: How long have you lived in this city?

mission.goal: Tell a neighbor how long you've been studying Italian.

say.en: I've been studying Italian for a year.

steps.title: Saying what you do
steps.how_to: How to say what your job is and what field you work in.
steps.intro: Today you'll answer one of the first questions people ask here: what do you do? There are a few ways to say it.

examples.said: E Lei, di cosa si occupa?
Sono ingegnere.
Lavoro come traduttrice.
Mi occupo di marketing.

steps.notice: Say your job with sono and no word for "a": sono ingegnere. You can also say lavoro come, or mi occupo di for a field.

ask.said: Che lavoro fai?
ask.en: What do you do for a living?

ask.said: In che campo lavori?
ask.en: What field are you in?

ask.said: Che lavoro vorresti fare in Italia?
ask.en: What job would you like to do in Italy?

answer.en: I'd like to work as a …

mission.goal: Tell a neighbor what you do for a living.

steps.title: Writing to an office
steps.how_to: How to open and close a short formal email.
steps.intro: Now you'll learn to start and end a short formal email to a school or an office. You can say it aloud or write it.

examples.said: Gentile dottoressa Rossi,
Le scrivo per chiedere informazioni sul corso.
examples.en: I'm writing to ask for information about the course.

examples.said: Cordiali saluti.
In attesa di una Sua risposta, Le porgo cordiali saluti.
examples.en: I look forward to hearing from you. Best regards,

steps.notice: Open with Gentile plus a title and surname, say why you're writing with Le scrivo per, and close with Cordiali saluti. Gentile works for a man or a woman.
steps.context: Anyone with a degree may be called dottore or dottoressa, so emails to offices open with Gentile, the title and the surname.

ask.said: Scrivi un'email alla segreteria della scuola. Come cominci?
ask.en: You're writing an email to the school office. How do you start?

ask.said: Vuoi sapere di più sul corso intensivo. Cosa scrivi nell'email?
ask.en: You want to know more about the intensive course. What do you write in the email?

answer.said: Le scrivo per chiedere informazioni sul corso intensivo.
answer.en: I'm writing to ask for information about the intensive course.

ask.said: Come chiudi un'email formale?
ask.en: How do you end a formal email?

mission.goal: Dictate the opening of an email asking about a course.

say.said: Gentile dottoressa Rossi, Le scrivo per chiedere informazioni sul corso.
say.en: Dear Dr. Rossi, I'm writing to ask for information about the course.

steps.title: Glad, sorry or afraid
steps.how_to: How to say how you feel about what someone else does.
steps.intro: Today you'll say how someone else's news makes you feel: glad, sorry or afraid. After these feelings, Italian uses the subjunctive.

examples.said: Sono contenta che tu sia venuto.
Mi dispiace molto che stia male.
examples.en: I'm so sorry he's not well.

examples.said: Ho paura che non arrivi in tempo.
examples.en: I'm afraid he won't get here in time.

examples.said: Mi fa piacere che ti trovi bene.
examples.en: I'm glad you're settling in well.

steps.notice: After a feeling plus che, the next verb is in the subjunctive, because it's how you feel about something, not a plain fact. For something already done, use sia plus the past: che tu sia venuto.

ask.said: Una tua amica è malata. Cosa le dici?
ask.en: A friend of yours is sick. What do you say to her?

answer.said: Mi dispiace che tu stia male.
answer.en: I'm sorry you're not feeling well.

ask.said: Un amico arriva a casa tua da Milano. Cosa gli dici?
ask.en: A friend arrives at your place from Milan. What do you say to him?

answer.said: Sono contento che tu sia venuto!

ask.said: Il tuo amico è ancora in viaggio e la cena è pronta. Cosa temi?
ask.en: Your friend is still on the way and dinner is ready. What are you worried about?

answer.said: Ho paura che non arrivi in tempo.
answer.en: I'm afraid he won't get here in time.

mission.goal: Tell a neighbor you're sorry her husband is ill.

say.said: Mi dispiace molto che stia male.
say.en: I'm so sorry he's not well.

steps.title: Glad to see you
steps.how_to: How to say how you feel about something you do yourself.
steps.intro: Now you'll say how you feel about something you yourself do: glad to see someone, sorry you can't come. Here Italian uses di and the plain verb.

examples.said: Sono contento di vederti!
examples.en: I'm so glad to see you!

examples.said: Mi dispiace di non poter venire.
Ho paura di non essere all'altezza.
examples.en: I'm afraid I'm not up to it.

examples.said: Sono contenta di avere una scusa per vedere Milano.
examples.en: I'm glad to have an excuse to see Milan.

steps.notice: When the person who feels and the person who acts are the same, use di plus the plain verb instead of che: sono contento di vederti.

ask.said: Un'amica torna in città dopo un anno. Cosa le dici?
ask.en: A friend comes back to town after a year. What do you say to her?

answer.en: I'm so glad to see you!

ask.said: Un amico ti invita a cena, ma hai già un impegno. Cosa gli dici?
ask.en: A friend invites you to dinner, but you already have plans. What do you tell him?

answer.said: Mi dispiace di non poter venire.

ask.said: Domani hai un esame. Come ti senti?
ask.en: You have an exam tomorrow. How do you feel?

answer.en: I'm afraid of getting it wrong.

mission.goal: Greet a friend you haven't seen in a while.

say.en: I'm so glad to see you!

steps.title: What great news
steps.how_to: How to react with "what a" in a few words.
steps.intro: Today you'll react to news in a word or two, the way people do the moment they hear it: what a shame, what luck. They all start with che.

examples.said: Che bella notizia!
Che peccato!
Che fortuna!

steps.notice: Che plus a noun, or che plus a describing word and a noun, makes an exclamation. There's no word for "a": che bella notizia.

ask.said: Un'amica ha trovato lavoro a Milano. Cosa le dici?
ask.en: A friend has found a job in Milan. What do you say to her?

ask.said: Un amico non può venire alla tua festa. Cosa dici?
ask.en: A friend can't come to your party. What do you say?

ask.said: Un amico ha trovato una casa in centro a buon prezzo. Cosa dici?
ask.en: A friend found a place downtown at a good price. What do you say?

mission.goal: React to a friend's good news.

steps.title: Good luck and best wishes
steps.how_to: How to wish someone luck or offer sympathy, and how to answer.
steps.intro: Now you'll learn the set phrases for big moments, each with its own reply: good luck, best wishes and condolences.

examples.said: In bocca al lupo per il colloquio!
Crepi!
Tanti auguri!
Le mie condoglianze.
examples.en: I'm so sorry for your loss.

steps.notice: These phrases come with set replies: you answer in bocca al lupo with crepi, and tanti auguri with grazie. Condoglianze is what you say when someone has died.
steps.context: Italians say auguri for birthdays, weddings, births and holidays, and in bocca al lupo before any exam or interview.

ask.said: Domani un tuo amico ha un esame. Cosa gli dici?
ask.en: A friend of yours has an exam tomorrow. What do you say to him?

ask.said: Un'amica ti dice: "In bocca al lupo!" Cosa rispondi?
ask.en: A friend says to you, "Good luck!" What do you answer?

ask.said: Oggi è il compleanno della tua vicina. Cosa le dici?
ask.en: Today is your neighbor's birthday. What do you say to her?

mission.goal: Wish a friend good luck before an exam.

say.said: In bocca al lupo per l'esame!
